title: Optimization of Tau PET Imaging for Alzheimer's Disease through Deep Learning-Based Image Reconstruction
text:
Positron emission tomography (PET) is a widely used imaging modality for Alzheimer's disease. This
project aims to develop advanced image reconstruction methods to improve Tau PET image quality.
Success of this project can enable better diagnosis and progression/treatment tracking of Alzheimer's
disease.

title: Employing Humanized Microbiome Mice to Understand Immune Activation and Translational Therapeutic Potential in Glioblastoma
text:
PUBLIC HEALTH RELEVANCE:
Immunotherapy (promoting an anti-tumor immune response) has demonstrated successful and exciting results
in certain cancers, but not in patients with glioblastoma, a malignant brain tumor. Additionally, the composition
of the gut microbiome has been shown to influence the efficacy of immunotherapy. Therefore, this proposal
seeks to identify optimal microbial gut compositions to rescue resistance to immunotherapy for patients with
glioblastoma.

title: Molecular Imaging of Peripheral and Central Nervous System Myelin
text:
Demyelinating diseases such as multiple sclerosis and Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease cause progressive nerve
damage and disability, yet clinicians currently lack effective tools to directly and noninvasively assess myelin
loss and repair. This project will develop a new PET imaging tool that can noninvasively and precisely detect
damage to the protective myelin coating on nerves—a key feature of diseases like multiple sclerosis and
Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease. By enabling doctors and researchers to see myelin health in real time, this
technology could greatly improve diagnosis, treatment monitoring, and the development of new therapies for
millions of people affected by demyelinating disorders.

title: Improving Native American Health Through Community-based Screening and Diagnostic Testing for Tuberculosis
text:
Among Alaska Natives in Alaska, tuberculosis (TB) remains endemic in communities and is a leading cause of
morbidity and mortality. Today, Alaska Native communities continue to have the highest rates of TB disease in
the United States, and most TB cases occur in villages that remain far from health centers. In this proposal, we
seek to evaluate the accuracy and feasibility of using several recent advancements for portable chest
radiography and non-invasive tongue swab sampling for the screening and diagnosis of TB disease within Alaska
Native communities.

title: Innovative Tools for Chemical Synthesis: Metal-Hydride Catalysis, Medicinal Motifs, and Molecular Probes
text:
This project will enhance our capability to invent therapeutics and subsequently prepare these medicines on
large-scale. Inspired by Nature’s catalyst, we develop ideal, environmentally friendly, and powerful ways to
transform simple building blocks (aldehydes, alkenes, and alkynes) into architectures relevant to medicine. Our
expertise in molecular design and synthesis will also be applied to address challenges at the interface of chemical
theory, fluorescent microscopy, and drug discovery.

title: Mathematical Model-Based Optimization of CRT Response in Ischemia
text:
We seek to understand the chronic effects of cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), HIS bundle pacing and
left branch bundle pacing under ischemic condition, which we will apply it to optimize CRT. The completion of
this proposal may significantly improve heart HF outcome and cost of management.

title: Technology development center for integrative physiologic models of the human musculoskeletal system
text:
We propose the creation of a musculoskeletal NAMs Technical Development Center (TDC) to advance the
development of combinatory physiological models for muscle, cartilage, tendon, and intervertebral disc
research. This initiative will enable the investigation of MSK pathologies while accounting for critical factors
such as environmental exposures, aging, and hormonal influences. By establishing a state-of-the-art research
hub focused on MSK NAMs development and broad dissemination, the TDC will usher in a new era of human-
relevant, ethical, and efficient biomedical research. It will serve as a transformative platform for exploring
disease mechanisms, assessing environmental toxicity, and advancing therapeutic interventions.

title: Mechanisms of Membrane Fusion
text:
Human infection by viral and bacterial pathogens is controlled by the HOPS protein,
which is conserved from yeast to humans and indeed throughout biology. We
discovered HOPS, purified it in its active form, and are continuing our intensive studies
of how it works. The insights into HOPS functions and the assays we developed for
studying HOPS will be central to understanding bacterial and viral pathogenesis and
may aid the future development of HOPS-targeted antibiotics.

title: Chronic ethanol drinking impairs limbic excitatory/inhibitory balance in monkeys and mice
text: Project Summary - P003 Although approximately 54% of Americans over the age of 18 consume alcohol, only 6.5% meet the criteria for an alcohol use disorder (AUD). Risk factors for Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) include a family history of alcohol use, genetics, stress and high drinking. Understanding the neurobiological mechanisms that may regulate the risk for and the response to harmful drinking is a focus of the Portland Alcohol Research Center (PARC). A continuing goal of the PARC is to understand the risk factors for and effects of chronic EtOH exposure on the tetrapartite synapse (i.e. presynapse, postsynapse, glia, and extracellular matrix (ECM)) that ultimately regulates neurotransmission. To this end P003, uses a brain circuitry approach focusing on the limbic cortico- striatal circuit due to its role in reward-based and motivational control over action selection. Additionally, in the current funding period, we found that heavy drinking (HD; i.e. consuming > 3g/kg daily on average, that is equal to 12 alcohol drinks in humans) and non-heavy drinking (NHD) rhesus macaques were differentiated by methylation signatures in the nucleus accumbens core (NAcC) and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC, Brodmann’s A32) that were associated with genes involved in the tetrapartite synapse. This ultimately corresponded to changes in glutamatergic (excitatory) and GABAergic (inhibitory) neurotransmission. Also, we found phenotypes of drinking and cognition that predicted or were a risk factor for HD. This continuing PARC project (P003) proposes to further leverage the rhesus macaque model of open access EtOH drinking to test the overall hypothesis that the difference in excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) balance within the limbic cortico- striatal circuit between NHD and HD contributes to EtOH-dose dependent adaptations in limbic neurocircuitry and associated behaviors. We will use to advantage the highly relevant and well- characterized nonhuman primate (NHP) alcohol drinking model in which rhesus macaques imbibe alcohol daily for 6 months and self-select into low and heavy drinkers. Additionally, our team will use multi-faceted approaches that include whole-cell patch clamp electrophysiology, expression of channelrhodopsin within the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC, A32/A34), chemogenetic expression of hM4Di in the NAcC, and in-cage assessment of drinking and cognitive behaviors. We will determine the extent to which chronic alcohol drinking alters excitatory-inhibitory balance within the limbic cortico-striatal circuit of macaques and mice (in collaboration with P002 and P004). We will explore whether manipulations to the presynaptic, postsynaptic, and ECM of the tetrapartite synapses can modulate the ethanol-induced changes in excitatory-inhibitory balance. Lastly, we will examine if the manipulations to the postsynaptic element and ECM that can restore excitatory-inhibitory balance can also decrease ethanol drinking and increase cognitive function.

title: Eco-evolutionary drivers of clonal dynamics during UV-induced skin carcinogenesis (PQ3)
text:
Cancers have readily-defined characteristics often referred to as “hallmarks”; however, the question of how the
sequence of cancer development progresses -- from normal tissue to carcinogen-damaged tissue to
precancerous lesion and finally to malignant tumors – remains unanswered. Classically, these steps are
attributed to the sequential acquisition of discrete genetic events such as driver mutations, but the clonal
dynamics governing cancer development happen over years, remain largely invisible even in model systems,
and have been difficult to link to specific molecular changes. Our long-term goal is to apply ecological and
evolutionary principles to cancer initiation and development in order to test whether the hallmarks of cancer are
acquired in three distinct phases each with distinct selective pressures and manifestations of cell competition
and cooperation.

title: The Role of HIF2 in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
text:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) responds poorly to immunotherapy and the mechanisms of this
resistance are unknown. We hypothesized that cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) mediate this intratumoral
immunosuppression in a HIF2-dependent fashion and provide evidence that HIF2 inhibition improves survival
in mouse models of PDAC by potentially improving immune responses. In this grant, we explore the
mechanisms of HIF2-dependent immune modulation by CAFs and perform preclinical studies to repurpose an
FDA-approved HIF2 inhibitor to improve the response of pancreatic cancer to immunotherapy.

title: When Plastic Meets Flow: Mechanobiological Consequences of Microplastic Exposure on the Endothelium
text:
Microplastic contamination is an emerging cardiovascular risk factor, with patients harboring detectable
microplastics in atherosclerotic plaques exhibiting an increased risk of myocardial infarction and stroke, yet the
mechanistic pathways remain undefined. This project will characterize microplastic effects on endothelial
mechanobiology under physiological flow conditions, examining disrupted cellular mechanics,
mechanotransduction signaling, and barrier function while testing therapeutic interventions. The research will
establish scientific foundations for cardiovascular risk assessment, generate preliminary data that can potentially
be utilized for clinical studies, and train undergraduate students in interdisciplinary environmental health and
cardiovascular research.

title: The function of PTEN
text:
To demonstrate how the catalytic domain of PTEN converts to a protein phosphatase. Determine how this
phosphatase regulates specific signaling pathways in response to growth and DNA damage.

title: A Deep Learning-based Assessment Pipeline for Peripherally Inserted Central Catheters (PICCs) on Pediatric Radiographs
text:
Peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs) have become an important part of clinical care for critically ill
children in pediatric intensive care units (ICUs). Unfortunately, improper positioning of the PICCs occurs in
approximately 3.6%-5.6% of pediatric patients. Thus, it is critically important to frequently assess the position of
PICCs. Chest X-rays (CXRs) are widely used radiographic images for the periodic assessment of PICCs in
children. However, assessing PICCs is a labor-intensive, time-intensive task for radiologists. Herein, we propose
to use artificial intelligence/deep learning techniques to automatically assess PICCs on CXRs from pediatric
patients. This will allow intensive care physicians to take timely remedies to reposition those improperly
positioned PICCs, thereby mitigating the potential risk of major clinical complications.

title: Predicting determinants of susceptibility to drug-induced arrhythmias
text:
Although all drugs must be tested for their potential to cause ventricular arrhythmia as an adverse event, the
probability of an arrhythmia depends on both the drug and the characteristics of the particular patient. This
research will advance the use of mathematical models to predict the risk of drug-induced arrhythmia, particularly
by developing a platform to assess how patient demographics and comorbidities interact with drugs to increase or
decrease personalized risk.

title: NaNOCure: A Nanotechnology-Based Topical Therapy for Infection Control and Enhanced Burn Wound Healing
text:
Second-degree burn wounds, exacerbated by antimicrobial-resistant (AMR) pathogens and biofilm formation,
result in heightened inflammation, impaired tissue regeneration, and delayed healing, ultimately increasing
wound care costs. NaNOCure, a nanoparticle-based nitric oxide (NO) delivery ointment, leverages the
synergistic antimicrobial (even against AMR bacteria), anti-inflammatory, and regenerative properties of NO to
promote rapid healing within a single deployable product. This scalable, user-friendly, and innovative solution
addresses the critical limitations of existing treatments, offering a significant advancement in burn wound care
and enhancing patient outcomes.

title: Fluorescence lifetime-based intraoperative imaging system for sarcoma surgeries
text:
There is an urgent need for imaging methods that can allow surgeons to distinguish cancer from heathy tissue
during surgery of bone and soft tissue sarcomas, to ensure that the tumor is fully removed and to preserve
healthy tissue and function. We will test an optical imaging system that captures differences between the
decay time of light emitted from tumors and normal tissue in patients who are injected with fluorescent dyes
and undergoing surgery of bone and soft tissue sarcomas.

title: Determination of pathogenetic mechanisms in cortex-specific Sucla2 deficiency as a model for mitochondrial encephalopathy
text:
Succinyl-CoA Synthetase (SCS) is a component of the Kreb Cycle, which is a central
feature of energy metabolism (the metabolic conversion of the building blocks of food
into a chemical energy source for the cell). Deficiency of SCS is a form of mitochondrial
disease that cause brain and muscle dysfunction that is associated with the reduction of
mitochondrial DNA content in the cell. This project establishes a model of SCS
deficiency in adult mice that will facilitate the exploration of SCS’s role in brain as well
as fundamental pathogenic mechanisms resulting from SCS deficiency.

title: Prediction of Biosensors to Small Molecules.
text:
Small molecules, such as metabolites, drugs, and environmental chemicals, play central roles in human
health and disease, yet most remain invisible to real-time monitoring in living systems. This project will
develop a universal, predictive platform based on a novel fluorescent protein scaffold (Synthetic UnaG
Biosensors) that directly couples small-molecule recognition to light emission. By enabling rapid
discovery of sensors for thousands of biologically and clinically important molecules, this technology
has the potential to transform biomedical research, accelerate drug development, and provide new
tools for precision diagnostics and monitoring public health.

title: The Role of Leiomodin1 in Hypoxic Neovessel Maturation
text:
Relevance: Scientists do not yet completely understand the molecular basis of peripheral artery disease
(PAD), a severe form of cardiovascular disease affecting 200 million people worldwide. Our preliminary studies
identify a potential novel association between smooth muscle cell expressed gene, Leiomodin 1, and PAD. By
understanding the underlying mechanism driving this potential association, our studies will likely lead to the
development of new strategies and therapies to effectively treat this increasingly morbid and mortal
pathological condition.
